questions.question: Independence gives $E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]$. Does $E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]$ conversely imply independence?
options: No; it only shows that $X$ and $Y$ are uncorrelated
Yes, because the joint law then factors into its marginals
Yes, if $X$ and $Y$ are discrete with finitely many values
No; the equality holds for every pair $X$, $Y$, so it says nothing

questions.question: For independent random variables $X,Y$ with finite variances, what is $\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)$?
options: $\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$
$\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)$
$\operatorname{Var}(X)\,\operatorname{Var}(Y)$
$\operatorname{Var}(X)-\operatorname{Var}(Y)$

questions.question: What events must be independent for random variables to be independent?
options: Only one selected pair of events
Only the events on which both variables are equal to zero
All generated events $\{X\in A\}$ and $\{Y\in B\}$
Only complements of the sample space

questions.question: If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, are $g(X)$ and $h(Y)$ independent?
options: Only if $g,h$ are linear
Only if $g=h$
Yes
No, never

questions.question: If independent discrete variables have $P(X=1)=0.3$ and $P(Y=2)=0.4$, what is $P(X=1,Y=2)$?
Two measurements taken from the same device may fail independence because of what?
options: Calibration drift affecting both measurements
Each measurement having its own random noise
Both measurements having the same distribution
Both readings being rounded to whole units

questions.question: Independent exponential clocks model what kind of situation?
options: Competing waiting times from separate sources
One nonconstant random waiting time used as the waiting time of both clocks
An unordered committee selection
A partition with empty cases

questions.question: Why is random-variable independence stronger than independence of one pair of events?
options: It only checks one single event for each variable
It ignores generated events
It requires the variables to be equal
It must hold for all suitable sets $A$ and $B$

questions.question: What does the notation $P(X\in A,Y\in B)$ mean?
options: The probability that $X$ equals the set $A$
The probability that $X$ falls in $A$ and $Y$ falls in $B$
The probability that $A$ and $B$ are independent variables
The probability of the sample space only

questions.question: What is a generated event for a random variable $X$?
options: An event unrelated to $X$
An event such as $\{X\in A\}$ determined by values of $X$
The expectation $E[X]$ only
Any subset of the sample space, whether or not $X$ determines it

questions.question: If $P(X\in A)=0.5$, $P(Y\in B)=0.2$, and $X,Y$ are independent, what is $P(X\in A,Y\in B)$?
If independent variables have $E[X]=2$ and $E[Y]=3$, what is $E[XY]$ under suitable integrability?
Why does having the same distribution not by itself imply independence?
options: Identical distribution forces generated events to factor
Same distribution means the variables are always separate sources
Independence is only about expectations
Variables can follow the same marginal pattern while still moving together

questions.question: Why can two measurements with a shared hidden drift fail to be independent?
options: Any two measurements taken at different times are automatically dependent.
Independence fails only when the two variables have the same mean.
A common drift can create shared randomness in both measurements.
Shared notation alone is enough to create statistical dependence.

questions.question: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two fair coin indicators from separate tosses. What is $P(X=1,Y=1)$?
Let $X$ be the head indicator and $Y$ the tail indicator from the same single fair coin toss. Why are they not independent?
options: They have no distributions
They are generated by separate tosses
Their marginal probabilities are negative
Knowing $X=1$ forces $Y=0$
